extracted.intended_audience: educated general public / readers of Popular Science Monthly interested in experimental physics and scientific explanation
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining an experimental physics phenomenon (the radiometer) in a popular-science magazine style: describing apparatus, contrasting rival hypotheses, reporting experiments and quantitative measurements, and relating results to established physical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and elimination of extraneous influences
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect test specimens and isolate the instrument from all extraneous influences (e.g., use a sealed glass bulb, exhaust air with a Sprengel pump to obtain a very high vacuum, hermetically seal the opening).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: films in early experiments were 'delicately suspended and carefully protected from all other extraneous influences'; use of Sprengel pump to reduce residual air to less than one-thousandth of original quantity before sealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design experiments to discriminate between competing hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct tests that will produce distinct predictions under different proposed mechanisms (e.g., direct mechanical action of light versus heat-engine action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle illustrated by the author's aim to test whether the radiometer's motion came from ether-wave impulses or from temperature differences between vane surfaces; Crookes deliberately 'abstained from speculating' to accumulate facts first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test proportionality to heating power (dose–response)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the effect scales with the heating (thermal) component of incident radiation rather than with visible light intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example experiment: interpose an alum-cell which transmits visible light but strongly absorbs heat-giving rays — motion was almost completely arrested despite bright light, indicating dependence on heating power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential vs concurrent action test on alternate surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether forces on opposite faces act differentially (opposite signs) or concurrently (additive), by selectively exposing blackened or lustrous faces and measuring resultant motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: screening so only black faces were exposed produced one speed, only lustrous faces another; numerical timing (seconds per ten revolutions) showed the effects were concurrent (sum nearly equals full exposure), supporting an internal heat-engine mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversibility test as diagnostic for heat-engine behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reversal of temperature gradients to see whether motion reverses — a reversible response is diagnostic of heat-engine operation between heater and cooler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: heating the glass bulb (making the glass warmer than vanes) then placing the instrument in a cold room caused the wheel to turn in the opposite direction until temperatures re-equilibrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary material properties (thickness, coatings) to probe mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Change vane material properties (e.g., thickness, diathermy, lampblack coating) to test hypotheses about absorption and heat transfer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: making mica vanes comparatively thick eliminated the effect of light on lustrous faces (thicker plate absorbed more heat), which supports the explanation based on differential heating rather than direct light-pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative measurement and repeatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Use precise, repeatable quantitative measurements (e.g., stopwatch timing of revolutions) and replicate observations to establish consistency and allow comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author measured time for ten revolutions repeatedly under different conditions and reported consistent times and converted them into comparable numbers of revolutions; repeated experiments on many instruments (>100) and variations were used to confirm conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider medium properties (pressure, density, molecular counts) and scaling limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the role of the surrounding medium: degree of rarefaction, molecular mean free path, and how these determine whether molecular/pressure effects will manifest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: effect appears only in highly rarefied atmosphere; author computes that less than one-thousandth of atmospheric pressure still leaves ~311,000 million million molecules per cubic inch and explains why molecular motion and momentum transfer only produce the observed reaction when air is highly rarefied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain phenomena using established theory (molecular/dynamical gas theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate experimental results to the mechanical/dynamical theory of gases (impacts and recoil of molecules, conduction vs convection) to provide a coherent theoretical account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author attributes radiometer action to gas-pressure differences caused by molecules rebounding with increased velocity from heated surfaces and explains why dense air masks the effect due to convection and diffusion; reconcile the new phenomena with prior molecular mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-of-magnitude and plausibility calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform back-of-envelope or more detailed calculations to check that observed magnitudes (pressures, temperature differences, forces) are sufficient to explain the motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: showing that a difference in pressure equal to one one-thousandth of atmospheric pressure (or a temperature difference of less than half a degree Fahrenheit) would be sufficient to account for the observed motion on the area of a vane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of deceptive appearances and subsidiary phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that chief effects can be obscured by subordinate phenomena and that initial appearances (e.g., apparent direct action of light) can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author warns how early deceptive appearances led eminent physicists to ascribe direct mechanical action to light; emphasizes that experiments can be honestly misinterpreted to support preconceived opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulate diverse experiments and avoid premature theorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect many variations and independent lines of experimental evidence before settling on an explanation; avoid biasing observations with prior theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crookes 'carefully abstained from speculating' while accumulating facts; the author tested over one hundred instruments under many conditions to reach a confident conclusion.
